title: Making V-Discs at NBC in Hollywood with Lena Horne, Hawkins and Krupa
summary: Every Monday the band records armed-forces disks hosted by actor Bubbles Whitman, on bills with Lena Horne, Coleman Hawkins and Gene Krupa's trio.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Anyway, we were in this club; I think we were there for four weeks. And while we were there, we... The War was still on, and we got this commission to do what was then known as Overseas Disks or...

V-disks, yeah, for the men overseas, for their entertainment. And we got a commission to do these things, and I think we did it for about three or four weeks. Every Monday, I think when we were off at the club, we would go into Hollywood at NBC Studios, and do these shows... This guy, Bubbles Whitman, who was a Black comedian in shows then... Actually, he was a movie actor, and he had been in a number of pictures where Black people were used then... Most of the times he was either in a picture, something of the Gone With The Wind type, where he would be a slave or a Big Jim or something like that -- in a servant capacity. Anyway, he was quite active in the movies, one of the most prominent Black actors then.
He MC'ed these shows, and they would have.... I remember one of the shows that was the Billy Eckstine band with Sarah
Vaughan, and Lena Horne was on it, and Coleman Hawkins had a group with Coleman Hawkins and Sir Charles Thompson, pianist, Denzil Best, the drummer...

No, it wasn't Oscar Pettiford. I don't remember who the bass player was. Then on another one, they had Gene Krupa. Gene Krupa had his trio then, and it featured Charlie Ventura on tenor saxophone and a pianist, Marty Napoleon. We would do these things every Monday, and they would record them or make transcriptions or something, and send them overseas for the soldiers as entertainment. Because there was no such thing as television during those days. Either they had live shows that went over, like shows that Bob Hope would take over, or else different organizations would do these disks.

I guess from the way our shows went, I'd imagine most of them were geared toward the Black soldiers or sailors or whatever. Anyway, later on, these transcriptions turned up, and now they can be bought as recordings. I think they were first found in Japan, and then later someone in England had them. But just what label they were under, I have no idea.
